title: Playlist Engine
tagline: One name holds a whole set of things, and you write the program that manages them.
objectives: Make a list, and get one thing out of it by its position.
Add to a list, take something out of it, and put it in order.
Read a few lines of Python that use a list, and say what they will print.

config.headline: One name. A whole set of things inside it.
lines: Last lesson every box held one thing: one name, one price, one number of seats. Today one box holds a whole set of things, in an order you decide. Python calls it a LIST.

The Studio's running order is a list. So is a seating plan, a cast, a shopping order and the set of songs a show plays between scenes. Once a set of things has one name, you can count it, add to it, take things out of it and put it in order — all without typing any of it out again.

**No music plays in this lesson, and none of these songs exist as sound.** A playlist here is a set of song TITLES you type, and the program you write manages the titles. Nothing you build today makes a noise.
You already have everything you need to start. A list is made the same way a box is made: a name, an = sign, and what goes in it. The only new part is what goes on the right of the =.
Here is the hour, in order.
First a short film with no sound, about six minutes, that shows a list as a rack of numbered boxes.

Then the Prediction Match. Somebody else in this room, at another computer, sees the same few lines of Python as you at the same moment. You both write down what you think it will print, you both lock it in, and then the code really runs.
You are not told who they are until the Match ends. You each get a call sign instead — a made-up name, like Director 3 — and that is the name on their screen and yours.
Then a second short film, then three builds where the program is finished for you less and less.
Then twelve minutes on your own Playlist Engine, with five songs you choose yourself.
It finishes with two short closing screens and a screen that asks you how the hour went.

config.title: Say what the code will do, before it does it
config.intro:
Reading code and knowing what it will do is a bigger skill than writing it, and the only way to practise it is to commit before you find out.

Six rounds. Somebody else in this room sees the same few lines as you, at the same moment. You each write down what you think it will print, you both lock it in, and then the code really runs on this screen.

**Getting one right is worth no points and getting one wrong costs you nothing.** The Match pays the same whatever you predict, as long as you play all six rounds. Being right is between you and your opponent.
steps: You are given a **call sign** — a made-up name like Director 3. That is the only name your opponent sees, and theirs is the only one you see.
Both screens show the same code. You each pick what you think it prints and lock it in.
The code really runs, and both predictions sit beside the real answer.
**Rounds 5 and 6 are on things nobody has taught you yet.** They say so before you see them, and they are worth nothing either way.

rounds.lead: A whole list, printed in one go. Look closely at what Python puts round it.
options: Opening Night Curtain Up Last Bus Home

Opening Night
Curtain Up
Last Bus Home
rounds.teach: Printing the whole list prints it the way Python writes a list down: square brackets round the outside, commas between, and speech marks round every title. It is one thing with one name, and that is what it looks like when you ask to see all of it.

rounds.lead: One box out of the rack. Count carefully, then type exactly what you think appears.
rounds.teach: Counting starts at 0, so playlist[0] is Opening Night and playlist[1] is Curtain Up. The number in the square brackets is a POSITION, never a count — this is the single thing people get wrong most often, all year.

len( ) counts how many things are in the list, so it says 3. The last POSITION is 2, because counting starts at 0 — the count and the last position are always one apart, and mixing them up is what causes most list errors.

rounds.lead: Two lines that look similar and do completely different things.
rounds.teach: .append( ) adds a new thing on the END and leaves everything already there alone, so the list grows from 2 to 3. That is the difference between adding and replacing: playlist = ["Last Bus Home"] would have thrown the other two away and left one.

rounds.ask: Have a guess. What will this print?
rounds.lead: Nobody has shown you this yet. Look at it, decide what you think happens, and lock it in.
options:
Opening Night
Curtain Up
Last Bus Home
rounds.teach: This is a LOOP. It takes the list one thing at a time, puts each one into a box called song, and runs the indented line underneath once for each of them. Three titles in the list means three trips round, and three printed lines. You build one of these yourself in about ten minutes.

rounds.ask: Have a guess. What will this print?
rounds.lead: Nobody has shown you this either, and this one catches nearly everybody.
rounds.teach: This is the trap. .sort( ) really does put the list in order — but it does it to the list ITSELF and hands nothing back. So the box called answer gets None, which is Python's word for nothing at all. Sort the list, then print the LIST. The second film says the same thing again, now that you have watched it happen.

sideShow.name: Margo
sideShow.alt: Margo, a cartoon theatre critic in a fur stole, peering over half-moon glasses
sideShow.open: Ah. An empty stage. I am Margo, and I review whatever is put in front of me. At the moment that is nothing.
lines: The silence continues. A bold artistic choice. Two stars.
I have now been staring at this waiting screen longer than I stayed for the second half of Hamlet.
Nothing is happening, and it is happening beautifully. One star.
In forty years of criticism I have never seen a stage this committed to being empty.
I would leave, but there is nowhere to leave to. I live here. This is my whole existence.
Half a star. And the half is generous.
echo: "{you}". I shall be honest: I have no idea what to do with that.
sideShow.exitLine: THEY'RE HERE! Five stars! A triumph! I take back everything! Go, go — do not keep them waiting!
sideShow.leaveLine: Leaving early? Everybody's a critic. Off you go.

config.intro:
Here is the whole shape of a playlist engine, on a running order that is not yours. Read it, press RUN, and watch what each line does to the rack.

Nothing on this card is for you to invent. It is here so that the shape is in front of you before you build one of your own.

errorWords.name: Python does not know a box with that name. Check the spelling on this line matches the name you gave the list further up.
errorWords.type: Python has been asked to put two different kinds of thing together, and it will not. If you joined a number onto words with a +, put str( ) around the number first. If you sorted a list with both numbers and words in it, Python cannot say which of them comes first.
errorWords.badinput: Python could not read that line at all. Check the speech marks come in pairs, the brackets come in pairs, and the line starts where the lines around it start.
errorWords.eof: Something was opened on that line and never closed. Look for a bracket or a speech mark with no partner.
errorWords.unindent: The lines inside the loop are not all lined up with each other. Every line inside a loop starts four spaces in, and they all start at the same place.
errorWords.index: You asked for a place in the list that is not there. Counting starts at 0, so the last place is one less than the number of things in the list.
errorWords.attr: There is no job with that name after the dot. Check the spelling of the word straight after the dot — append, remove, sort and insert are the ones you have.
errorWords.timelimit: That program was still going after a few seconds, so it was stopped. Something in it is repeating and never finishing.
errorWords.other: Python stopped at the line named above. Read that line again, slowly, and check every bracket and every speech mark.
errorWords.value: Python could not use the thing in the brackets. If this was a remove line, the title has to match one that is really in the list, capital letters and all.

builds.goalLine: Write a playlist engine that does five things to five songs of your own.
builds.brief: Start with five real song titles you would put in a show. Then make the program add one more, take one out, pick one at random to announce, put the whole list in order, and print the first three under a heading that says Now Playing.

features.label: It ADDS a song, so the list ends up longer than the one you typed.
features.nudge: Your list is not growing. Look for the line with append on it, and check the title you are adding is inside speech marks.

features.label: It TAKES ONE OUT, so one of your songs is gone by the end.
features.nudge: Nothing is being taken out. remove needs a title spelled exactly as it appears in your list — including the capital letters.

features.label: It picks a song AT RANDOM and announces it.
features.nudge: Your program prints the same thing every time. Look at whether random.choice is really being used, and whether the line above it imports random.

features.label: The list ends up in A to Z order.
features.nudge: Your list is not in order at the end. Look at where your sort line is: anything that changes the list AFTER it can put it out of order again.

features.head: now playing
features.label: It prints a Now Playing heading and then exactly THREE of your songs.
features.nudge: Look at the two lines that print the top three: the heading has to say Now Playing, and the loop has to take the first three only.

shape: print( a line that announces random.choice( <list name> ) )
print( a heading with Now Playing in it )
builds.shapeNote: The order matters: anything that changes the list after the sort line can put it out of order again.
builds.matchedSay: All five. Send your Now Playing card to the person you played against.
builds.notYetSay: Not all five yet. The list on the right says which. Read the console for anything Python could not do.

builds.title: Job 1 — only the ones by one artist
builds.whiff: A taste of next year: the program decides which ones to print.
builds.goalLine: Print only the titles that have the word Live in them.
builds.brief: A loop can look at each title and decide whether to print it. The word if is how a program chooses, and you meet it properly next year — here it is, doing one job.

lines.t: playlist = ["Opening Night", "Curtain Up (Live)", "Last Bus Home", "The Long Way Round (Live)"]

builds.matchedSay: Two lines out of four titles. The if line is what made the loop choose.

builds.title: Job 2 — play it backwards
builds.whiff: One line turns the whole running order round.
builds.goalLine: Print the list with the titles in the opposite order.
builds.brief: Lists have a job called reverse, and it works exactly like sort: it changes the list itself and hands nothing back.
builds.matchedSay: Reversed. And the line you left behind would have printed None, for exactly the same reason sort does.

builds.title: Job 3 — what else can go in a list?
builds.whiff: An experiment. Lists are not fussy.
builds.goalLine: Put a number and some words in the same list, and print each one on its own line.
builds.brief: A list will hold anything, and it will hold different kinds of thing at the same time. Build it and see what comes out.
builds.matchedSay: Three lines, and one of them is a number. A list does not care what is in it — but ask for a place that is not there and it stops.

config.waitingSay: Your program has stopped and is waiting for you to type an answer. The box is just above this button. RUN wakes up again as soon as the program has finished.

config.intro: One last question, and this one IS marked. Your teacher sees how the class did on it, so answer it on your own.

items.stem: Your list holds five titles. You run the line `playlist.append("One More")`. What is true afterwards?
options: The list holds one title, because append replaced what was there
The list holds six titles, with One More on the end
The list holds five titles, and One More was printed instead
The list holds six titles, with One More at the front

config.help: One marked question about the job you used most today. You are told whether you were right, and why, at the very end of the lesson — after the How did it go? screen.

config.intro:
Last one, and it is three lines. Put them in the order that prints every title in the list, one on each line.

Click a line on the left to move it across, or drag it. You get one go, and you are shown the working order afterwards either way.

item.prompt: A working loop needs the list to exist first, then the for line, then the printing line that sits inside it.

config.doneText: Correct. The four spaces in front of the last line are what put it inside the loop.
config.help: Click a line on the left to move it into Your program, or drag it across. Press Check my program when you are sure. You get one go, and the working order is shown to you afterwards whether you were right or not.

config.alreadyFiled: You have already sent this to your teacher. You can read back through it as often as you like, and nothing you click now will change what you sent.
config.offlineSay: Your connection is playing up, so your answers are safe on this computer and will send by themselves. That is the lesson finished.
statements: I can make a list, and get one thing out of it by its position.
I can add to a list, take something out of it and put it in order.
I can read a few lines of Python and say what they will print.
config.help: Under each sentence, click the button that says how today really went. Then, at the bottom of the screen, click how hard the hour felt. The comment box goes to your teacher and nobody else. Everyone finishes this screen before leaving — it is how your teacher hears from everyone, not just the loudest.
